evidence.claim: The name Alligator does not settle what this earthen figure represents.
evidence.quote: Lepper suggests that the Alligator Mound is an effigy of an underwater panther, a powerful figure in Native American myth.

evidence.claim: In 1999, Brad Lepper and Tod A. Frolking investigated the mound and dated charcoal from its base, estimating construction at about AD 950.
evidence.quote: In 1999, Brad Lepper and Tod A. Frolking conducted a professional archaeological investigation of the mound.  By radiometric dating of a piece of charcoal recovered from the base of the mound, they estimate its construction to have been 1,000 years BP (about AD 950).

evidence.claim: Lepper suggests that the figure represents an underwater panther from Native American myth.
evidence.quote: Lepper suggests that the Alligator Mound is an effigy of an underwater panther, a powerful figure in Native American myth.

evidence.claim: He thinks early European settlers misunderstood a description of a fierce water creature and assumed it meant an alligator.
evidence.quote: He thinks that early European settlers misinterpreted what Native Americans told them about the effigy.  They were told that it was a fierce creature that lived in the water and ate people, which they assumed to be an alligator.

evidence.claim: It is one of two surviving effigy mounds known in Ohio, along with Serpent Mound.
evidence.quote: Alligator Mound is one of two extant effigy mounds known in the present-day state of Ohio, along with Serpent Mound in Adams County, Ohio.
